newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai finmin sees austerity producing results.
newsitem.headline: Thai finmin sees austerity producing results.

text.p: Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan on Wednesday voiced confidence that recent austerity measures focusing on government budget cuts would brighten the county's economic outlook this year.
Amnuay told the foreign chambers of commerce he sees sound fiscal and monetary policies as long-term solutions for Thailand's current account deficit and export problems.

"I can detect a surge in confidence (by the private sector) ...I believe we have started on the right footing," Amnuay said, referring to sharp rallies of Thai stocks on Tuesday and Wednesday after the government announced major budget cuts.

The minister said he had full support from Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, who is also Defence Minister, in curbing military spending as government planners struggled to curb the current account deficit which rose to a six-year high of 8.2 percent of gross domestic product in 1996.
Amnuay, a non-elected minister and respected economist, has set a target to narrow the deficit to 7.5 percent to 7.9 percent in 1997 and gradually lower in subsequent years.
The minister has said he would seek to cut at least 50 billion baht ($2.0 billion) of the national budget in each of the 1996/97 and 1997/98 fiscal years.
He said military acquisition projects being affected include plans to buy a satellite, submarines and armoured vehicles. He said these projects alone had been slated to cost over 50 billion baht.
A 50 billion baht cut in government spending would represent about 5.1 percent of the current national fiscal budget of 984 billion baht.

Amnuay, stressing the need for austerity measures, said however: "You don't want to see Thailand going into a financial shock. I have to give the doses as the financial doctor (but) I don't want to put tax money to support speculators. I don't believe in market intervention."
The minister made the statement when asked if the government would intervene to prop up the battered stock market which tumbled 35 percent last year.

Amnuay stressed it was essential for both the Thai government and private sector to tighten their belts in a joint effort to improve the economy which expanded 6.7 percent in 1996 -- its slowest pace in 10 years.
"As a country, we should not spend beyond our means both in consumer and public spending," he said.
He pointed out that Thailand's total foreign debt has risen to almost $90 billion, of which about 82 percent was tapped by the private sector.
